article_title: The Design and Validation of the Quantum Mechanics Conceptual Survey
citation: McKagan, S. B., Perkins, K. K., & Wieman, C. E. (2010). The Design and Validation of the Quantum Mechanics Conceptual Survey. https://arxiv.org/abs/1007.2015
title: The Quantum Mechanics Conceptual Survey (QMCS), a 12-question research-based conceptual survey of quantum mechanics
description: The QMCS is a 12-question multiple-choice survey measuring students' conceptual understanding of quantum mechanics, intended, in the authors' words, "to measure the relative eﬀectiveness of diﬀerent instructional methods in modern p hysics courses". It was developed iteratively over roughly three years through faculty interviews, textbook and syllabi review, student observations and interviews, expert review, and statistical analysis. It is a survey rather than a concept inventory, covering a broad but partial range of modern physics topics.
requirements: Must be protected from student access so questions remain secure; it is distributed by password on request from the authors
constraints: Most appropriate for assessment as a posttest only in sophomore-level modern physics courses; not appropriate for assessing graduate courses
Contains only 12 questions, which the authors state is too few to adequately probe understanding and causes discretization of scores
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of quantum mechanics (relationship between mathematical description and the physical world)
examples: Administered in class as pretest and posttest in modern physics, junior quantum, and graduate quantum courses at multiple institutions
Questions adapted from prior research instruments such as the QMVI and from literature on student difficulties
key_sources: McKagan, S. B., Perkins, K. K., & Wieman, C. E. (2010). The Design and Validation of the Quantum Mechanics Conceptual Survey. https://arxiv.org/abs/1007.2015

article_title: Surveying students' understanding of quantum mechanics in one spatial dimension
citation: Guangtian Zhu and Chandralekha Singh. (2011). Surveying students' understanding of quantum mechanics in one spatial dimension. http://goo.gl/tSKuK
title: Quantum Mechanics Survey (QMS): a 31-item multiple-choice conceptual survey of one-dimensional quantum mechanics
description: The QMS is a 31-item multiple-choice survey assessing the conceptual framework of quantum mechanics of one particle in one spatial dimension, covering possible wavefunctions, bound and scattering states, measurement, expectation values, stationary states, the role of the Hamiltonian, and time dependence. The authors state: "we developed the Quantum Mechanics Survey (QMS), a 31-item multiple-choice test." Items were developed from instructor consultations, free-response questions, think-aloud interviews, and statistical item analysis, with distractors built from common misconceptions.
requirements: Administered after a junior/senior-level course has covered the relevant one-dimensional quantum mechanics topics; students need to understand the basics of linear algebra but no complicated mathematics
constraints: The authors state the survey "is not appropriate for such courses in which all relevant concepts are not covered", such as one-semester courses or courses beginning with two-state systems
target_learners: First-year graduate students in quantum mechanics
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding of non-relativistic quantum mechanics of a single particle in one spatial dimension
examples: Administered to 226 students in 14 classes across ten universities, with item difficulty and point biserial discrimination computed for each item
key_sources: Guangtian Zhu and Chandralekha Singh. (2011). Surveying students' understanding of quantum mechanics in one spatial dimension. http://goo.gl/tSKuK

article_title: Improving Students' Understanding of Quantum Mechanics by Using Peer Instruction Tools
citation: Chandralekha Singh and Guangtian Zhu. (2010). Improving Students’ Understanding of Quantum Mechanics by Using Peer Instruction Tools. 2010 PERC Proceedings. https://www.compadre.org/PER/
title: Bank of about 500 research-based QM concept test questions
description: The authors have developed "about 500 research-based concept test questions which are in the multiple-choice format" for quantum mechanics, building on their prior research on student difficulties and misconceptions. The questions typically focus on conceptual aspects rather than computation: some expect basic calculus and linear algebra, but complicated mathematical manipulations are not involved in any of them.
requirements: Developed through an iterative process informed by research on QM student difficulties and misconceptions
constraints: Complicated mathematical manipulations are not involved in any concept tests
target_learners: advanced undergraduate and graduate quantum mechanics students
examples: CT1-CT3 on bound and scattering states for 1D potentials, used in a junior-senior level QM course
key_sources: Chandralekha Singh and Guangtian Zhu. (2010). Improving Students’ Understanding of Quantum Mechanics by Using Peer Instruction Tools. 2010 PERC Proceedings. https://www.compadre.org/PER/

article_title: Categorization of Quantum Mechanics Problems by Professors and Students
citation: Shih-Yin Lin and Chandralekha Singh. (2016). Categorization of Quantum Mechanics Problems by Professors and Students. https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.02947
title: Use problem categorization tasks in quantum mechanics courses as a tool for understanding the patterns students see when contemplating how to solve problems
description: The article proposes that asking students to group quantum mechanics problems by similarity of solution reveals the patterns a learner perceives in problems, extending the classic categorization methodology to upper-level quantum mechanics. It states that "The categorization of problems by students in a quantum mechanics course can be a useful tool for understanding the patterns students see in a problem when contemplating how to solve it." The task asks participants to create their own category names, justify groupings, and optionally place problems in multiple categories.
requirements: Participants must generate their own category names and justify why problems belong together, rather than sorting by difficulty.
constraints: Faculty categorizations of quantum mechanics problems are diverse rather than uniform, so there is no single agreed-upon expert key against which to score student responses.
target_learners: upper-level undergraduate physics students in quantum mechanics courses
target_learning_goals: organizing quantum mechanics knowledge by concepts and procedures relevant to problem solving
examples: 22 students in two honors-level quantum mechanics courses categorized 20 problems in 35-40 minutes as a quiz; six faculty categorized the same problems, and three faculty scored all categorizations as good, moderate, or poor.
key_sources: Shih-Yin Lin and Chandralekha Singh. (2016). Categorization of Quantum Mechanics Problems by Professors and Students. https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.02947

article_title: Assessing Expertise in Quantum Mechanics using Categorization Task
citation: Shih-Yin Lin and Chandralekha Singh. (2016). Assessing Expertise in Quantum Mechanics using Categorization Task. https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.02948
title: 20-problem quantum mechanics categorization task with three-column response sheet
description: A categorization instrument consisting of 20 quantum mechanics problems adapted from end-of-chapter exercises in commonly used upper-level undergraduate textbooks, administered with a three-column response sheet. The first column asks for a category name, the second for a description explaining why the problems group together, and the third for the problem numbers in each category. Problems may be placed in more than one group, solving is not required, and grouping must be based on features of the problems rather than difficulty.
requirements: Instructions specifying grouping by similarity of solution, not by difficulty level
A response sheet with category name, description, and problem-number columns
constraints: Administered here as a class quiz on the last day of two honors-level quantum mechanics courses, with full quiz credit for participation
target_learning_goals: assessing expertise and knowledge organization in quantum mechanics
examples: Students were given approximately 35-40 minutes to complete the task; all but one faculty member completed it in less than 30 minutes
key_sources: Shih-Yin Lin and Chandralekha Singh. (2016). Assessing Expertise in Quantum Mechanics using Categorization Task. https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.02948

article_title: The impact of peer interaction on the responses to clicker questions in an upper-level quantum mechanics course
citation: Ryan Sayer, Emily Marshman and Chandralekha Singh. (2016). The impact of peer interaction on the responses to clicker questions in an upper-level quantum mechanics course. https://scholar.google.com
title: Peer instruction sequence: individual clicker response, 1-2 minute peer discussion in groups of two or three, individual re-response, then whole-class discussion
description: In this case study, after lectures tailored to difficulties reported in pre-lecture reading summaries, students answered multiple-choice concept tests individually (ICT) without seeing a response histogram, then discussed "in groups of two or three for 1 -2 minutes" and tried to convince their peers, then individually answered the same question again (GCT), followed by a whole-class discussion. Clickers counted as a bonus 2.5% of the total grade, with 80% of points for participating and 100% for correct answers.
requirements: Students answer individually before discussion and again individually after discussion
Groups are formed from students' usual seated collaborations
Time is reserved for both ICT and GCT administration
constraints: Both ICT and GCT were administered only during the first six weeks of the course due to time constraints, and not for all clicker questions even then
target_learners: upper-level undergraduate physics students (juniors and seniors)
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of quantum mechanics topics such as the hydrogen atom, identical particles, and perturbation theory
examples: The instructor browsed students' reported difficulties from pre-lecture reading summaries and tailored the in-class lecture and clicker questions to address those challenges
key_sources: Ryan Sayer, Emily Marshman and Chandralekha Singh. (2016). The impact of peer interaction on the responses to clicker questions in an upper-level quantum mechanics course. https://arxiv.org/abs/1701.01415

article_title: Teaching quantum mechanics to over 14,000 nonscientists
citation: J. K. Freericks, L. B. Vieira, D. Cutler, and A. Kruse. (2019). Teaching quantum mechanics to over 14,000 nonscientists. https://www.edx.org/course/quantum-mechanics-everyone-georgetownx-phyx-008-01x
title: Browser-based JavaScript/WebGL simulation framework with modular virtual quantum experiments, released under LGPL 2.1
description: The course's tutorials are built on a custom simulation engine using standard browser features: "The maturity of JavaScript and WebGL in modern browsers (desktop and mobile) is a key factor for our success." The framework features "visually-distinct modular devices, with inputs and outputs, which may be attached to one another, rotated and labeled at will," letting developers quickly assemble many experimental setups. Particles released by sources pass through devices to detectors, where results are tallied in bar charts, and a probabilistic model automatically computes the expected virtual-experiment results. The tutorials are freely available for download under the LGPL 2.1 license on the authors' GitHub repository.
requirements: Must rely only on standard and widely deployable features of major web browsers, avoiding third-party software such as Java or Flash
constraints: The authors note Java programs suffer from numerous security concerns and there is no web interface to run cT programs, motivating the browser-only approach
target_learners: students on computers, tablets and phones
target_learning_goals: visualize abstract quantum phenomena and run virtual quantum experiments
examples: Fig. 2 shows a virtual setup with an atom source, Stern-Gerlach analyzer, gate, quantum eraser, and analyzer loop feeding detectors D1 or D2
key_sources: J. K. Freericks, L. B. Vieira, D. Cutler, and A. Kruse. (2019). Teaching quantum mechanics to over 14,000 nonscientists. https://www.edx.org/course/quantum-mechanics-everyone-georgetownx-phyx-008-01x

article_title: Analyzing the structure of basic quantum knowledge for instruction
citation: Giacomo Zuccarini. (2023). Analyzing the structure of basic quantum knowledge for instruction. https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.04231
title: Survey on incompatibility and compatibility of observables developed from the observable-relation maps
description: As a research application of the framework, the article reports that "the maps on the relations between two observables have been used to develop a survey on incompatibility and compatibility". The maps may serve as a basis for the design of investigations into student understanding, and this survey instantiates that use for the maps addressing measurement on an eigenstate of an observable, where compatibility, incompatibility, degeneracy and the kernel of the commutator structure the pathways of solution.
requirements: The survey derives from the maps on the relations between two observables, which require knowledge of a formal representation of the eigenstate concerned
target_learning_goals: assessing student understanding of compatibility, incompatibility and commutation relations between observables
examples: The article cites the Michelini and Zuccarini 2014 PERC study on university students' reasoning on physical information encoded in quantum state in connection with this research line.
key_sources: Giacomo Zuccarini. (2023). Analyzing the structure of basic quantum knowledge for instruction. https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.04231

article_title: Epistemic stances toward group work in learning physics: Interactions between epistemology and social dynamics in a collaborative problem solving context
citation: Jessica R. Hoehn, Julian D. Gifford, and Noah D. Finkelstein. (2020). Epistemic stances toward group work in learning physics: Interactions between epistemology and social dynamics in a collaborative problem solving context. https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.02425
title: Hour-long focus group session of four modern physics students solving quantum mechanics problems (the case study dataset)
description: The dataset is a video and transcript of a one-hour focus group in which four students (Penny, Morgan, Cam, Sarah—pseudonyms) from a modern physics class worked on prepared QM problems, including an infinite square well problem and a double square well problem. Students were recruited by email, framed as exam preparation but not grade-connected (extra credit offered), organized by scheduling constraints, and monetarily compensated. Three focal episodes (from the beginning, 17 minutes in, and 46 minutes in) were selected for discourse analysis.
requirements: Video recording and full transcription with conventions for pauses, gestures, and interruptions
constraints: One-time session with one group in the last week of the semester; the fourth student, Sarah, made very few verbal contributions and her social dynamics were outside the scope of the paper
target_learners: undergraduate modern physics / quantum mechanics students
target_learning_goals: mathematical sense making in quantum mechanics
key_sources: Jessica R. Hoehn, Julian D. Gifford, and Noah D. Finkelstein. (2020). Epistemic stances toward group work in learning physics: Interactions between epistemology and social dynamics in a collaborative problem solving context. https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.02425

article_title: Validation and Administration of a Conceptual Survey on the Formalism and Postulates of Quantum Mechanics
citation: Emily Marshman and Chandralekha Singh. (2020). Validation and Administration of a Conceptual Survey on the Formalism and Postulates of Quantum Mechanics. https://www.appendix.org/assessments/assessment.cfm?A=QMFPS
title: Quantum Mechanics Formalism and Postulates Survey (QMFPS), a 34-item validated multiple-choice conceptual survey
description: The QMFPS is a 34-item multiple-choice conceptual survey assessing students' understanding of the formalism and postulates of quantum mechanics, including Dirac notation, the Hilbert space, state vectors, Hermitian operators, compatible and incompatible observables, quantum measurement, time dependence, expectation values, and spin angular momenta. It fills a gap because previously developed QM surveys do not focus explicitly on these topics. The final version is available on PhysPort, and it can be completed in one 50-minute class period.
requirements: Students should have learned Dirac notation; the survey is appropriate as an upper-level undergraduate post-test or graduate pre/post-test
Students need to understand the basics of linear algebra since that is central to the formalism and postulates of QM
constraints: It should not be administered as a high-stakes test and the data should be interpreted for the class as a whole
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of the formalism and postulates of quantum mechanics
examples: Administered to 464 students from 6 institutions over four years; 350 undergraduate and 114 graduate students
key_sources: Emily Marshman and Chandralekha Singh. (2020). Validation and Administration of a Conceptual Survey on the Formalism and Postulates of Quantum Mechanics. https://www.appendix.org/assessments/assessment.cfm?A=QMFPS

article_title: Validation and Administration of a Conceptual Survey on the Formalism and Postulates of Quantum Mechanics
citation: Emily Marshman and Chandralekha Singh. (2020). Validation and Administration of a Conceptual Survey on the Formalism and Postulates of Quantum Mechanics. https://www.appendix.org/assessments/assessment.cfm?A=QMFPS
title: Upper-level QM learning goals should include QMFPS concepts and connect conceptual understanding with mathematical formalism
description: Because students in traditionally taught courses can hide lack of conceptual understanding behind mathematical skills, the authors argue that quantum mechanics instruction should close the gap between conceptual and quantitative problem solving. They suggest learning goals for upper-level QM include proficiency in the concepts covered by the QMFPS and emphasize the connection between conceptual understanding and mathematical formalism, with graduate instructors reflecting on student responses to design instruction accordingly.
requirements: Course assessments should not focus only on quantitative reasoning, since even graduate students may not be motivated to develop a coherent knowledge structure if they do
target_learning_goals: functional (conceptual plus quantitative) understanding of quantum mechanics formalism and postulates
examples: Courses using active learning techniques such as peer instruction, tutorials, cooperative group problem solving, and Just-In-Time-Teaching were associated with better QMFPS performance
key_sources: Emily Marshman and Chandralekha Singh. (2020). Validation and Administration of a Conceptual Survey on the Formalism and Postulates of Quantum Mechanics. https://www.appendix.org/assessments/assessment.cfm?A=QMFPS

article_title: A study on pre-service physics teachers' conceptualization on elementary quantum mechanics
citation: Glauco Cohen Ferreira Pantoja. (2017). A STUDY ON PRE-SERVICE PHYSICS TEACHERS' CONCEPTUALIZATION ON ELEMENTARY QUANTUM MECHANICS. Investigações em Ensino de Ciências – V22 (2), pp. 120-138. https://doi.org/10.22600/1518-8795.ienci2017v22n2p120
title: Concept-sequence pattern for elementary Quantum Mechanics: Physical System → Dynamical Variables → State → Time Evolution, anchored in three situations
description: A unit-level instructional pattern for teaching elementary Quantum Mechanics conceptually rather than only mathematically. The most general concept, Physical System, is taught first, followed by Dynamical Variables, State of a Physical System and Time Evolution, so that "Physical System (the most general) → Dynamical Variables → State of a Physical System → Time Evolution" facilitates progressive differentiation and later integrative reconciliation. Each concept is introduced through one of three situations — the Stern-Gerlach experiment, the hydrogen atom and the ammonia molecule — with the situation presented first, then the concepts, then differentiation and reconciliation, repeated for each situation.
requirements: Presentation of situations belonging to different areas of Physics to facilitate concept acquisition
Dirac notation used as representation so mathematics is not eliminated
constraints: The authors note teaching of State of a Physical System and Time Evolution is rarely found in bibliographic reviews, limiting prior guidance
target_learners: undergraduate physics students taking introductory Modern Physics
target_learning_goals: concepts of Physical System, Dynamical Variables, State of a Physical System and Time Evolution
predictivity and causality evoked by Time Evolution
examples: A 12-hour didactic approach with six undergraduate physics students, all taking introductory Modern Physics for the second time, using pencil-and-paper problems, field notes and concept maps as research instruments
key_sources: Glauco Cohen Ferreira Pantoja. (2017). A STUDY ON PRE-SERVICE PHYSICS TEACHERS' CONCEPTUALIZATION ON ELEMENTARY QUANTUM MECHANICS. Investigações em Ensino de Ciências – V22 (2), pp. 120-138. https://doi.org/10.22600/1518-8795.ienci2017v22n2p120

article_title: From Computing to Quantum Mechanics: Accessible and Hands-On Quantum Computing Education for High School Students
citation: Qihong Sun, Shuangxiang Zhou, Ronghang Chen, Guanru Feng, Shi-Yao Hou, and Bei Zeng. (2024). From Computing to Quantum Mechanics: Accessible and Hands-On Quantum Computing Education for High School Students. arXiv:2403.17485. https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.17485
title: Correspondence mapping between quantum mechanics postulates and quantum computing concepts
description: The course is organized around a mapping, illustrated in Table I, that "provides a straightforward mapping to facilitate understanding" between the postulates of quantum mechanics and quantum computing concepts: the wavefunction postulate corresponds to the qubit, the unitary-evolution postulate corresponds to quantum logic gates, and the measurement postulate corresponds to the readout process. This mapping underpins the course's strategy of teaching computing concepts first and showing afterwards how they are underpinned by quantum mechanical principles.
requirements: Instructors pair each quantum mechanics postulate (state, evolution, measurement) with its quantum computing counterpart (qubit, gate, readout) when introducing the concepts.
constraints: The mapping covers the state, evolution, and measurement postulates as illustrated in Table I; other postulates are not mapped in the article.
target_learners: high school students with limited computer science background
target_learning_goals: understand how qubits, gates, and measurement are underpinned by quantum mechanical principles
link theoretical concepts with practical uses
examples: Table I maps the wavefunction postulate to the qubit |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩, unitary evolution to quantum logic gates, and measurement collapse to obtaining |0⟩ or |1⟩ at readout.
key_sources: Qihong Sun, Shuangxiang Zhou, Ronghang Chen, Guanru Feng, Shi-Yao Hou, and Bei Zeng. (2024). From Computing to Quantum Mechanics: Accessible and Hands-On Quantum Computing Education for High School Students. arXiv:2403.17485. https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.17485
